content_voiceover: The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoidal because of cooperative binding across the four heme subunits — binding the first oxygen increases affinity for the next. Curve shifts are a classic board topic. A left shift means increased oxygen affinity, so hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly and releases less to tissue; causes include decreased temperature, decreased 2,3-DPG, decreased hydrogen ion and CO2, that is alkalosis, plus fetal hemoglobin, methemoglobin, and carbon monoxide. CO both shifts the curve left and directly reduces oxygen-carrying capacity, which is why CO poisoning causes severe tissue hypoxia despite a normal-looking saturation reading. A right shift means decreased affinity and more oxygen unloaded to tissue, driven by increased temperature, increased 2,3-DPG, and increased hydrogen ion and CO2 — the Bohr effect — which is adaptive because exercising, acidic tissue is exactly where oxygen delivery is needed. Clinically, stored blood loses 2,3-DPG and shifts left, impairing oxygen delivery after transfusion, while chronic hypoxia raises 2,3-DPG to shift the curve right.
keypoints: CO poisoning: left shift + ↓O2 capacity → severe hypoxia
Stored blood ↓2,3-DPG → left shift, impaired delivery
keypoint_voiceover: Key points on the dissociation curve. It's sigmoidal due to cooperative oxygen binding. Left shift means increased affinity — from decreased temperature, decreased 2,3-DPG, alkalosis, fetal hemoglobin, methemoglobin, and carbon monoxide. Right shift means decreased affinity and more oxygen delivered — from increased temperature, increased 2,3-DPG, and acidosis, the Bohr effect. Carbon monoxide poisoning causes a left shift plus reduced oxygen capacity, producing severe hypoxia. Stored blood loses 2,3-DPG, shifting left and impairing delivery after transfusion.
